Why isn’t the economy growing?. DURING the roughly 150-year period between 1760 and World War I, England, the countries of northwest Europe, and the US went through the economic transformation of the Industrial Revolution. Real per capita GDP, which had remained stagnant at $2-3 per day, started to rise. Real wages that had historically remained slightly above subsistence level doubled. The percentage of labour force employed in agriculture plummeted. The West’s share of global manufacturing — around 25 per cent before the Industrial Revolution — jumped to more than 80pc by 1914. Some economic historians have labelled this shift as humanity’s ‘great escape’ from poverty, disease, and squalor. In the past 200 years, Japan, South Korea, and China stand as the only non-European nations to have bridged the economic divide with the West. These countries accomplished in decades what the West achieved in centuries by sustaining long periods of nearly double-digit economic growth. After the destruction wreaked by World War II, Japan grew at an average annual rate of nearly 10pc from 1955 to 1973. In 1968, it surpassed Germany to become the second largest economy. Starting in the early 1960s, South Korea entered a period of sustained economic growth, described as the ‘Miracle on the Han River’. Real GDP increased 25-fold in three decades. In 1996, South Korea became a member of the OECD. In the 40 years following the ‘reform and opening up’ of 1978, China’s economy grew at an average annual rate of about 9.5pc, increasing the size of its GDP roughly 35- to 40-fold in real terms. In the process, China lifted nearly 800 million people out of poverty and became the world’s largest economy in PPP terms in 2014. The high-speed economic growth of the East Asian economies displayed three characteristics. First, the period of rapid economic growth was preceded by fundamental restructuring of society’s political and cultural institutions. Second, the shift from an agricultural to industrial economy was spearheaded by the state. Third, during the transformation period, the attainment of econo­m­­ic goals was prioritised over political freedoms. For Pakistanis to live better, the economy must grow at near double-digit rates for decades. From 1945 until 1951, Gen Douglas MacArthur presided over Japan’s post-World War II transformation as supreme commander of the allied powers. He had Emperor Hirohito issue a rescript denouncing his divinity, promulgated a new constitution, carried out land reforms, changed the education system, and introduced American cultural elements to Japanese life. In South Korea, before Gen Park seized power in 1961, land reforms had already been accomplished through the initiative of the United States Army Military Government in Korea. Gen Park launched the New Community Movement, promoted traditional ethno-nationalism, and strictly regulated social life. During the first 30 years after the revolution of 1949, the Communist Party of China dismantled the 2,000-year-old imperial system, gave land title to nearly 300m peasants, and laid the foundations of a modern state. The post-World War II reconstruction in Japan was led by the ‘iron triangle’ of bureaucrats from the trade and industry ministry, Liberal Democratic Party politicians, and the captains of Japan’s leading industrial conglomerates. In South Korea, Gen Park adopted the policy of export-led economic growth by providing subsidised credit to chaebols, suppressing domestic demand, and quashing labour unions. In China, the state laid the foundations of basic and heavy industry through financial and technical Soviet assistance. Even after Deng Xiaoping’s liberalisation, the state still controls strategic sectors of the economy and takes the lead in pioneering new technologies. Nominally, Japan was a parliamentary democracy during the post-World War II economic tra­n­s­­formation, but the Liberal Democratic Party re­­mained in power for 38 years in what is described as a ‘one-and-a-half party system’. Following a coup in 1961, Gen Park first ruled South Korea as a military dictator and then adopted a constitution giving him near absolute powers without term limits. China has remained a one-party-led state since its founding in 1949. Deng Xiaoping, who launched the economic ‘reform and opening up’ in 1978, rejected dem­ands for Western-style democracy and suppressed the 1989 demonstrations in Tiananmen Square. In varying degrees, these conditions were present in all countries that successfully transformed into industrialised nations. Pakistan experienced something similar during its first two decades, when it attempted land reforms, passed the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, and adopted the five-year planning system, with input from the Harvard Advisory Group. All the economic and social gains of these early decades were lost starting in the 1970s. In 1998, Pakistan discontinued the practice of drawing five-year plans and began transitioning to a medium-term development framework. Slow growth in the last two decades has caused Pakistan to fall behind its South Asian neighbours in living standards. The manufacturing sector represents less than 13pc of GDP, and the country runs an average annual trade deficit of around $30 billion. Harsh policy measures have stabilised Pakistan’s economy. During FY2024-2025, Pakistan recorded a current account surplus because of import restrictions and robust remittances. Fiscal deficit dropped to a multi-decade low of 2.6pc of GDP in 2025-26. Record-high inflation has come down to more manageable levels. Pakistan’s sovereign credit rating has improved because of lower external risks. However, growth has remained stagnant at around 3.5pc per annum for the last decade. The IMF projects an annual growth rate of 3.5pc for 2026-27, which is barely sufficient to offset the depreciation of the capital stock and compensate for population growth. For Pakistanis to experience any meaningful improvement in living standards, the economy needs to grow at near double-digit rates for several decades. Our current subsistence level agricultural economy with a rudimentary level of industrialisation has reached the limits of its productive capacity. Transformative growth can only come by making the quantum leap to industry. However, industrialisation requires us to fundamentally restructure the political and social order of society, and the state should lead the industrialisation process, with political differences subordinated to the pursuit of economic goals. The poverty trap will not be broken by incremental policy reforms. It requires restructuring the entire system of society. The writer has a background in public administration. He has worked with international financial institutions, including the World Bank. Published in Dawn, September 18th, 2026

Restructuring lessons. INTERIOR Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s proposal for more provinces wasn’t the first time someone close to the establishment made the suggestion. However, this time a stated motivation was also provided: namely, the complete collapse of the existing governance system. While much has been written about this issue, it has largely been theoretical and speculative, with the closest real-world examples coming from other countries. The problem with those examples is that, while informative, they mostly exist in a context very different to Pakistan’s, making it difficult to draw parallels. But an example closer to home can help us predict better. The last time Pakistan’s internal borders were redrawn was in 2018 with Fata’s merger with KP through the 25th Amendment. A similarly stated motivation for the merger was given at the time — the utter collapse of the old Fata governance system. That system has been blamed for the militant takeover in many parts of Fata (now called the merged districts). Many also hold it responsible for erstwhile Fata’s extremely poor human development indices compared to the Pakistani average. The merger with KP, and thus the extension of KP’s institutional structures, laws, and systems, was deemed necessary to resolve Fata’s problems. Another proclaimed benefit was that the merger would bring the government closer to the public. The state believed that the militants had filled the void created by an unresponsive government. So, in many ways, the motivation to merge rested on two beliefs: first, to replace an old, collapsed system with one offering better governance; and second, to involve communities in decision-making by bringing government closer to them. Similar justifications are now being touted to support the idea of new provinces. Eight years after the merger, the question is: how effectively has the change improved both aspects for residents of the merged areas? The question of whether decision-making has been brought closer to the people and thereby made government institutions more responsive to the public’s needs is perhaps the easier one to answer: there’s no evidence that matters have improved; if anything, the opposite appears to be true. The merged areas still have no share in the NFC and continue to depend on discretionary federal funding. In fact, they are a step removed from that planning process, as it must come through KP rather than directly to them. Similarly, the tribal system is, by definition, participatory and community-led. Replacing it with a more centralised, institutional state structure has decreased community involvement and the power of the local people to run their own affairs. The question of governance is more complex, but even here, there is not much improvement. First, the new system is less participatory even in governance, further alienating people from their government. Second, the administrative system is now far too bureaucratic to respond promptly. It is increasingly bloated — current administrative expenditures for the merged areas have more than doubled, from about Rs50 billion at the time of the merger to over Rs100bn now. Similarly, the judicial process, like elsewhere in the country, is painfully slow, making locals increasingly likely to turn to traditional jirgas rather than the courts. The creation of alternative dispute resolution me­­chanisms and dispute resolution councils, aligned with traditional jirgas and under the guise of the district administration and district police respectively, acknowledges the delay in dispensing justice. Worse, there has been no marked improvement in any human development indicator; apart from isolated instances, no real examples of systemic improvement in service delivery exist. Where security is concerned, there is a surge in militant activity in the region , with terrorist incidents and casualty figures worse than in the years before the merger. Clearly, the merger is not preventing the resurgence of militancy in the area. What insights does the Fata merger offer into the recently proposed move to create new administrative units? The merger failed to achieve the improvements that proponents vowed it would bring, even though it had backing at the national level, unlike the idea of new provinces, especially from the three major national political parties (the PML-N, PTI and PPP), establishment experts and development partners. It was a rare moment in Pakistan’s recent political history in which all three major national parties came together to pass the 25th Constitutional Amendment and then saw it passed in the KP Assembly by consensus. The idea of new provinces has no such national consensus at the moment; it would look more like arm-twisting if the political parties go ahead with it. However, even in the case of the merger, locals were excluded from the decision-making process, and a majority of Fata’s elected parliamentarians at the time favoured reforms, though they raised serious reservations about how these reforms were being pursued. This was cause for concern. Regrettably, their alarm was disregarded; in fact, it was termed a vain effort by locals to save an archaic system. One might argue that the merger was, in many ways, a different reform than creating new provinces. Yet both reforms ignore the same basic issue of structure and approach, which must be addressed before there is any redrawing of internal provincial borders or creation of new administrative units. To have a responsive government, communities need more involvement through a regularly functioning, well-resourced local government system. Helping communities decide the policies they want is essential for a successful transition to new systems. Whether this happens in a larger administrative unit or a smaller one matters less. Most importantly, Pakistan needs a mindset shift in how it pursues policy and reforms. We need an approach that replaces preconceived notions and unsubstantiated beliefs that dictate policy. We must move away from a mindset that envisions the state as a mere administrative entity; instead, the state must assume the role of a citizen-empowering force that serves the people. Without this, even the most logical ‘reforms’ will prove cosmetic and do little to address systemic failures. The writer is a development practitioner and a former parliamentarian. SBP rejects rumours about Rs10 banknote. KARACHI: The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) on Thursday explicitly den­ied social media rumours claiming the Rs10 banknote is being phased out or that there is a set deadline for its discontinuation. The central bank said social media is trying to dispute the issue by setting a specific deadline for discontinuing the Rs10 banknote. The SBP categorically refuted reports circulating on social media about the purported discontinuation of the Rs10 banknote and the last date for its exchange. “The reports are baseless and without substance,” said the SBP. “The SBP has submitted a proposal to introduce a new banknote series, which is currently under consideration by the Federal Cabinet,” it said, adding that the matter remains under deliberation and that no decision has been taken on replacing or discontinuing any denomination. “Any such decision, if taken, will be formally communicated to the public through official channels, and adequate time will be given to the public to exchange discontinued banknotes,” the SBP said. On Aug 25, SBP Deputy Governor Dr Inayat Hussain briefed the Senate Standing Committee on Finance and Revenue, reportedly saying the SBP is considering a phased withdrawal of the Rs10 banknote because of rising printing costs. Additionally, the SBP is developing a new design for the Rs5,000 note to strengthen anti-counterfeiting measures. Published in Dawn, September 18th, 2026

Court orders NCCIA to probe Rs4.8m ‘unauthorised’ transactions from Gul Plaza victim’s account. KARACHI: A sessions court on Wednesday directed the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) to investigate an alleged “unauthorised” transaction of Rs4.8 million from the bank account of a Gul Plaza fire -affected shopkeeper and submit a report within 45 days. Shopkeeper Muhammad Shahzad filed an application under Sections 22-A and 22-B of the Code of Criminal Procedure before Additional District and Sessions Judge (South) Abdul Zahoor Chandio, seeking registration of an FIR over an unauthorised transaction from his account in a private bank. The applicant claimed that he had a shop at Gul Plaza, which was destroyed in the fire. He stated that the Sindh government had provided Rs7 million in financial assistance to help him re-establish his business. SBP directed to examine whether banks complied with digital banking security requirements; reports sought within 45 days However, he claimed that on June 26, Rs1 million was transferred to the bank account of Muhammad Safdar and, the very next day, Rs3.8 million was transferred to the account of Samiullah without his authorisation or knowledge. He denied sharing his bank account credentials or password with anyone. On the other hand, the private bank informed the court that the disputed transactions were executed through its digital app and that its internal investigation found that the activity had originated from the applicant’s own device. The bank also took the position that the “transactions occurred through the use of confidential credentials”. After hearing all sides, including representatives of the private bank, NCCIA and the complainant, the court directed the director general of the NCCIA to conduct a comprehensive investigation in accordance with the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) and all other applicable laws and submit a report within 45 days. The court directed the investigating officer (IO) to preserve all records relating to the disputed or alleged “unauthorised” transactions from the applicant’s account. It also directed the private banks holding the beneficiary accounts, as well as the bank where the applicant maintained his account, to preserve all records related to the alleged transactions. The court ordered the State Bank of Pakistan to examine the matter from a regulatory perspective and determine “whether the concerned banks complied with the applicable digital banking security requirements and whether any regulatory proceedings have been initiated or are warranted” and submit a report within 45 days. “The object of these directions is not merely recovery of the applicant’s money. The banking system operates upon public confidence and the protection of customers against unauthorised electronic transactions is an essential component of that confidence. The regulatory framework itself recognizes the need for effective security controls in digital banking and provides mechanisms for regulatory enforcement where those controls are not properly implemented,” the court observed. Mir Raza commission reprimands first investigator over ‘zero work’. • Justice Sial says the investigating officer tried to make it a ‘suicide’ case • Holds him responsible for destroying evidence; calls him unfit for police service • Asks a victim’s business partner to meet Raza’s family, answer their questions and submit the replies to commission KARACHI: The commission formed to investigate the circumstances and possible negligence in the Mir Raza Ali murder case on Thursday deplored that the first investigating officer had hardly made any effort to probe the matter and did not fulfil legal formalities during the investigation. It also noted that most of the paperwork and procedures were carried out by police officers other than the former IO, including the inquest report, collection of CCTV footage and questioning of suspects. The one-member commission headed by Justice Omar Sial of the Sindh High Court further noted that the police had improperly interrogated people as 33 persons’ statements were recorded out of which the first IO had only questioned 10 individuals while he had also kept the samples taken after the autopsy in his custody for several days. It said that since some allegations were levelled against Karachi Police chief Azad Khan and DIG Amir Farooqui — who is heading the current investigation team — during the testimony of the police surgeon, the commission would send questionnaires to both the senior police officers and asked the counsel for the aggrieved family, Jibran Nasir, to submit questions, if any, in this regard by Monday. The victim’s business partner Ahmed Bhardey along his lawyer also appeared on Thursday after the commission summoned him for giving interviews to some journalists and claiming that he had much more to tell, but the commission had not allowed him to do so. Justice Sial directed Bhardey to meet the family members of the victim privately and answer all their questions and also submitted the same before the commission with his affidavit while the commission also warned his lawyer from scandalising it. The first IO of the case Inspector Shabbir Ahmed Laghari appeared and deposed that he had joined the police in 2002, investigated 20 to 25 cases so far and he was assigned the investigation of the case on July 28 at around 3:20pm by the senior investigating officer (SIO) of Ferozabad police station Arshad Javed. Thereafter, the former IO deposed that he had visited the victim’s house, went to three or four places in the neighbourhood, but no footage could be obtained and on July 29, SHO Ferozabad Adeel Afzal and the SIO had informed him about recovery of the victim’s body, which was already shifted to hospital. He further testified that he had visited the hospital where ASI Nadeem Mughal of Gulistan-i-Jauhar police station had carried out the formalities of Section 174 (inquest report) of the criminal procedure code and also collected samples from the medico-legal officer and handed the same over to him (Laghari) on July 30. He said that the following day, he along with SIO Ferozabad and police staff had visited the crime scene, where the body was found, it was not secured as the crime scene unit had yet to arrive there. Inspector Laghari also stated that a blood-stained flowerpot was recovered at the scene and the same was sent to the laboratory for analysis, but he did not prepare the seizure and inspection memos. When asked as to why crime scene was not timely secured, he asserted that it was the responsibility of the Gulistan-i-Jauhar police station to protect the same and added that a bullet casing was found from the crime scene by the then SHO Gulistan-i-Jauhar Kamran Qureshi. Justice Sial asked him as to why SHO Adeel Afzal was taking more interest in the case as he had collected footages and visited the crime scene on July 28 despite the fact that he was not authorised to do so as it was the responsibility of the IO. The first IO replied that the SHO often appeared to be active in order to assist the investigators as the investigation section lacked resources and manpower. He conceded that all footage was provided to him by the SHO, but seizure memo was not prepared since the same were shared on the WhatsApp. At this juncture, the commission observed that he has done zero work regarding investigation of the case so far and he should not be serving in police for such conduct. When Justice Sial asked Inspector Laghari as to why the samples collected during autopsy on July 29, had been submitted to the laboratory on Aug 6, he replied that he had received the samples from ASI Mughal on July 30 and kept in his personal possession till Aug 6 instead of Malkhala of the police station due to want of post-mortem report since samples could not be deposited without the report. He also asserted that the police had faced difficulties in obtaining the autopsy report and eventually, such report was received on Aug 3, on the following day the laboratory was found closed, the staff of lab had raised some objections on Aug 5 and therefore, the samples were deposited on Aug 6 after addressing such objections. He further said that he had not prepared seizure memo in this regard. When the commission asked him that he did not find anything suspicious about the individuals grilled by police including gardeners, a rickshaw driver or others among 33 persons. He asserted that as per the nursery employees, the body could not have been thrown from any direction at the crime scene and apparently, he might have walked there himself. Inspector Laghari also attempted to defend the version of gardeners and claimed that they might not have heard the gunshot despite being close to the crime scene due to traffic buzz. At this juncture, Justice Sial came down hard on him and said that he was also trying to make it a case of suicide and hardly made any effort to probe the case or collect evidence while collection of footages and codal formalities were carried out by other police officers. The commission also noted that the first IO had not prepared various important memos, many entries were also not made in daily diary of the police station and violated procedures of investigation. It further said that the statements of these 33 persons were not recorded properly as key questions were not asked while the statements of gardeners were hardly containing 10 lines. Justice Sial said that former IO had not obtained DVR as videos were only available in his mobile phone which was not admissible whereas all the witnesses had given a different account while he was telling an entirely different story and also equally responsible for destroying the evidence. Inspector Laghari replied that he had faced difficulties during investigation since he had fallen ill and his daughter was admitted to the hospital during these days. However, Inspector Laghari said he had never stated that it was a case of suicide and he had incorporated Sections 302 and 201 of the Pakistan Penal Code in the case. The phone of victim was recovered by SHO Adeel Afzal, the memo was prepared by ASI Faisal Nadeem and the phone as well as smartwatch of the victim had been sent for analysis on Aug 12. Thereafter, he said that the investigation of the case was transferred to DSP Siraj Lashari and all the relevant record was handed over to him. Adjourning the hearing till Sept 21, the commission said that it was issuing notices to various police officers who were part of the first and second investigation teams to record their deposition next week. LNG shortages hit Pakistan badly. BANGKOK: Pakistan is among the worst-hit nations by liquefied natural gas (LNG) disruptions due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and could future-proof its domestic energy and power supply by increasing its focus on renewables and coal. “Qatar and the UAE together supply about 99pc of Pakistan’s LNG — mostly for power generation, fertiliser production and industrial use. LNG accounts for about 30pc of total gas supply,” said the Gastech Conferences in its report ‘The Outlook for Gas and LNG Markets in Asia’ released at its 54th annual event. It said that beyond addressing immediate challenges, policymakers in Asia may now be reviewing how to future-proof domestic energy and power systems with renewed focus on energy security. This could be done by accelerating renewables, such as swift-build, utility-scale solar, wind farms and commercial rooftop solar, plus storage deployment. They would also be looking at speeding up investment in long-term infrastructure, including gas storage and updating power generation mixes and giving gas plants better flexibility. Gastech report notes US-Iran war has redrawn global energy maps This is where Pakistan’s Universal Gas Distribution Company (UGDC) held discussions with several international firms on potential projects, including gas storage, long-term LNG supplies and gas distribution in overseas markets, its Chief Executive Officer Ghiyas Abdullah Paracha said. The Gastech report said the countries were also examining options for expanding operating reserves to ensure grid agility for unexpected events and rethinking fuel stockpiles by expanding strategic stocks for transport fuels and power generation. The nations may also be looking at boosting cross-border power export/import options to share shortages. The report said the Middle East’s fluid landscape — as demonstrated by the conflict involving Israel, the United States and Iran which began in February and the resultant bottleneck in the Strait of Hormuz — has redrawn global energy maps in real time and further highlighted the geopolitical sensitivity of gas and LNG markets. Gastech noted that gas supply disruptions have prompted Pakistan’s government to look to coal, hydropower, and nuclear power, while price volatility and shipping uncertainty are likely to sharply increase power costs. Ghiyas Paracha told journalists that his company received a greater-than-anticipated response at the conference. “We have got understanding with some companies that have shown interest in building gas storage facilities in Pakistan. Some companies have shown keen interest in long-term LNG contracts with UGDC,” Paracha said. Paracha said UGDC’s participation at Gastech was also significant because the company was presenting Pakistan’s gas-sector reforms and the opening of the country’s gas market to private-sector participation at an international energy forum. South Korea rules out deployment of troops for military intervention in Iran. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Friday that US President Donald Trump clearly wants dialogue with Pyongyang and confirmed Seoul will not be deploying troops to intervene militarily in the US-Israeli war on Iran. Trump, seeking to revive the bond he claims to have forged with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in his first term, said last month that he plans to meet Kim later this year. The US president also said it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons. Seoul says there are around 80 to 120. North Korea, which has secured critical backing from Russia in recent years, did not clearly respond to Trump’s overtures. Lee said on Friday it was “clear” that “Trump wants dialogue, and I am also urging President Trump to engage in dialogue.” South Korea — which Pyongyang has repeatedly labelled as its adversary —was continuing “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between North Korea and the United States, Lee told reporters at the presidential Blue House. He added that such a meeting “remains difficult … but is not impossible”. “I cannot say for certain how likely it is, but it is also clear that we must make every possible effort to turn that possibility into reality,” he said. South Korea and the US held a shorter edition of their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercises last month, following an order from Trump to scale them back. The truncated drills and Trump’s overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that Seoul could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North. Seoul has also committed to $350 billion in US investments under a deal struck last year to avoid the worst of Trump’s tariffs, but specific projects and final terms are still being negotiated. Lee said on Friday the negotiations had been “very complex and difficult”, adding that while the two sides were said to be close to agreement, he had found some terms “difficult to accept” and talks were continuing. ‘No, thank you’ The South Korean president also said that Seoul will not deploy troops to intervene militarily in the war on Iran. “There will be no involvement or intervention in the war. We will not deploy troops or military assets in that manner,” said Lee. Lee’s answer follows reports that Seoul was weighing a possible deployment to the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key flashpoint in the war. He added that South Korea will “carry out the minimum necessary activities” to protect its own merchant ships and oil shipping routes. Lee reiterated three times that South Korea would not deploy troops in a way that could lead to military intervention. “We have upheld the principle of non-involvement and non-intervention in the war until now,” he said. “And we will continue to uphold it going forward.” Trump complained in an interview late last month that Washington had received “very little help” from other countries, singling out South Korea — its key security ally in Asia — as an example. “We help them, but when it came to helping us, I didn’t put on a heavy sell, but I just said, ‘Would you like to participate?’” Trump said in an interview with Fox News. “And they all said, ‘No, thank you.’ And I said, ‘I’m going to remember that to myself,’” he added. The US stations about 28,500 troops in South Korea to bolster the country’s defences against the nuclear-armed North Korea. However, Trump’s repeated criticism of time-honoured alliances has cast doubt on US commitments to security in East Asia. Lee also ruled out seeking to extend his constitutionally limited single term in office, amid mounting criticism after he and some allies floated constitutional reform. His approval ratings have fallen to record lows in recent weeks amid growing discontent over his real estate policies, controversial personnel appointments and concerns over stock market volatility.

'Our commitment is unconditional': Amid Houthi attacks, DG ISPR says Pakistan will 'go to any extent' to defend Saudi Arabia. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said that Pakistan will go to “any extent” to defend Saudi Arabia, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. He made the remarks in an interview with Arab News , clips of which were posted on its social media account on X on Friday. The remarks come as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis has intensified, with the group making gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast near the strategic waterway and launching missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory, while Riyadh has stepped up airstrikes against Houthi positions. This week, the Saudi-led coalition battling the Houthis accused the rebels of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world. However, the Houthis swiftly rejected Riyadh’s report as a “lie”. “Pakistan fully stands with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia, both diplomatically and physically. And I would like to underscore the word physically,” Lt Gen Chaudhry said in the interview with Arab News . “We will go to any extent for the security of Haramain Sharifain and the kingdom of Saudi Arabia. To any extent as asked and required by our Saudi brothers,” he said. “It should be clear that the people of Pakistan stand shoulder to shoulder with their Saudi brothers and sisters. There should be no doubt about it,” he said. “So, in a nutshell, we are there and will continue to defend the kingdom of Saudi Arabia against any aggression,” he said. The military’s spokesperson added that Pakistan’s politico-military leadership remained in continuous contact and engagement with the Saudi leadership. He said that at the same time, Pakistan, “very earnestly and sincerely”, was working with the help of regional countries and others to find a “negotiated, peaceful outcome of this complex situation”. “That’s where the position of Pakistan is,” he said. In another clip posted on X, he said Pakistan “remained not only committed, but we are already there for the protection of Haramain Sharifain and the kingdom of Saudi Arabia”. “We are there to protect them,” he asserted, reiterating that Pakistan would “go to any extent” as required by the Saudi leadership. “Our commitment to Saudi security is unconditional. It stems from a deep-rooted, historical and unbreakable bond between the people of Pakistan and the people of Saudi Arabia, between the political and the military leadership of both countries,” he said. “So, nothing stops us. Nothing bars us. Nothing is there which hesitates [sic] our commitment. So, whatever is required, whatever is asked, we will go to any extent for that,” he said. According to the write-up of the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked about the phone call between Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday. “The politico-military leadership of Pakistan remains in continuous communication with the esteemed leadership of the kingdom of Saudi Arabia on all these matters,” he was quoted as saying by the publication. Lt Gen Chaudhry added that Islamabad was consulting regional governments to seek “a negotiated and peaceful outcome” to the wider crisis. He described the Islamabad memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran in June as “a consensus document which we think provides the only real pathway forward for getting out of this complex military situation in which we are’. According to the publication, asked whether Pakistan expected to bring Washington and Tehran back to negotiations soon, the military spokesperson gave no timetable. He said Islamabad continued to search for common ground despite mistrust, “spoilers” and “detractors”. Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had signed the “ Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement ” in Riyadh last September, pledging that any attack on either nation would be treated as an act of aggression against both. Last month, the countries and Turkiye also signed the Makkah Defence Alliance, which stipulates that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. Its inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years. Earlier this week, Lt Gen Chaudhry said that the Makkah defence pact had no “regional aspirations” and that it was intended for collective deterrence. “It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said in an interview with Al Arabiya English. Meanwhile, Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan on Thursday reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitments to Saudi Arabia’s security, but stressed that the Houthi conflict should be addressed through dialogue and diplomacy rather than through coercive means. “The Houthis must also stop their activities, and in this regard, our discussions basically revolve around bringing peace and stability through dialogue and diplomacy, and not through coercive measures,” he said. The FO spokesperson also said that Pakistan was committed “in intent and spirit” to implementing the agreements signed with Saudi Arabia. He nevertheless declined to disclose how Pakistan might respond operationally, saying such decisions involved matters of confidentiality.

Unlikely political bedfellows team up against Albanese over staff. While they wouldn’t normally be caught dead together, Pauline Hanson, Fatima Payman and Dai Le have held a joint press conference to take aim at the prime minister.
Migration changes to hit students’ families and working holiday makers. The long awaited overhaul comes as new figures show net migration continuing to fall.

Why the story of urchin barrens and kelp forests is more complex than we thought. Sea urchins eat kelp – but new research shows their diets and relationships with kelp forests are more complex than commonly thought.

Life just got tougher for international students under new visa rules. Why is this group being targeted?. The federal government will make it harder for international students to bring their families with them to Australia, among other changes.

Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain hides deep caves that can teach us about alien worlds. It might appear featureless, but one of the world’s largest limestone regions hides a remarkable underground world.

Australia’s ‘barking mad’ bet on nuclear submarines – the AUKUS deal five years on. On The Conversation Weekly podcast, defence and security analyst Hugh White explains why the AUKUS project has been anything but smooth sailing.

Friday essay: how Australia’s ‘invasion novels’ have reflected our cultural anxieties around race. Foreign ‘invasion plots’ have featured in Australian literature for more than a century. Though critiqued by some authors, fears of white erasure endure.

7 of the weirdest things coffee does to your body. Coffee doesn’t just make you feel more alert. Here’s what else happens when you drink a cuppa.
Making a claim at the Fair Work Commission? These are the new AI rules you need to follow. Trusting AI too blindly could end up costing you money – and see your legal case dismissed.
From war to weather, Australian farmers are planting spring crops in an uncertain world. Growers across the country are grappling with surging fuel prices and inconsistent rainfall.

We found the hidden force that created two chains of underwater volcanoes running side by side. A new study unearths the deep Earth connection between Lord Howe Island and its sibling chain of drowned volcanoes.

How rural policing gaps can make escaping domestic violence harder. Rural and regional areas bear a disproportionate burden of domestic violence. Distance, police staffing and station hours aren’t the only barriers to seeking help.
The International Olympic Committee wants mental health screening in elite sports. Here’s why. The mythology of the bullet-proof athlete often obscures the reality of elite sport’s mental toll.

Russia’s parliamentary elections will not be a referendum on the Ukraine war – or anything, really. Russia is convening its first national parliamentary elections since invading Ukraine, which offer a great deal of predictability but also some unexpected surprises.
As AI reshapes jobs and workers change industries, employers need to be more flexible too. Most career changers rely on their networks to move to a new industry, new research shows.

I love my skincare routine. Do I have a body image problem?. Spending time on skincare can be enjoyable, creative and soothing. But sometimes this self-care can be concerning. Could it be ‘cosmeticorexia’?

The government’s migration policy prioritises knee-jerk politics over careful planning. The government’s migration policy announcement was long-awaited, but the contents ultimately fell short of expectations.
It’s getting easier to live off-grid – but it comes with certain costs. People who have extra funds, suitable homes and a desire to be self-sufficient may consider disconnecting from the grid.

On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/11/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 11 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky E-post Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Spara Utskrift 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. But the latest exchanges underscore a mutual willingness to use military escalation and economic disruption in gambits to strengthen positions at the negotiating table. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. While Israel has reduced the intensity of its attacks, it persists in conducting lethal strikes in the south, where it continues to occupy territory. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the continued Israeli assaults undermine the historic direct diplomacy that is happening between Israeli and Lebanese officials. Left unchecked, Israel’s attacks could sour relations between Tehran and Washington even further, making it even more difficult to reverse the escalatory cycle that has taken off in the Gulf. 10 July 2026 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva Monday by reiterating a call for a ban on what are called Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, arguing that “some decisions must remain forever human – none more than taking a human life”. Crisis Group expert Issandr El Amrani says it is urgent to regulate the use of AI in warfare: AI-aided weapon systems are enabling rapid processing of targets with decreased human oversight, with potentially grave consequences for civilians, as seen during Israel’s war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. These “killer robots” need not be fully autonomous to render human oversight largely meaningless. More than 120 states, mostly from the Global South, have endorsed such a ban. But countries that have this technology, including the U.S., the UK and Russia, oppose it, contending that current provisions under international humanitarian law are sufficient. CHINA China test-fired a long-range ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine in the South Pacific Monday, its first such exercise in these waters in two years. Beijing characterised the missile test as part of routine annual training that comports with international law, stressing that it was not directed at another country. Australia, Japan and New Zealand raised objections, however, with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong calling the test “destabilising” for the Asia Pacific and Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara describing it as “a grave concern” for the world.
