CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht Q&A / Asia-Pacific 11 September 2026 12 minutes An Historic Poll Puts Peace to the Test in the Philippines In mid-September, residents of the Bangsamoro in the southern Philippines will elect regional parliamentary representatives. In this Q&A, Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht explains the importance of this step in the peace process between the national government and ex-rebels in the region. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Georgi Engelbrecht Senior Analyst, Philippines https://twitter.com/Durian_Diaries Related Tags Philippines What is happening? On 14 September, over two million residents of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao will elect their parliament for the first time. The vote is a milestone in the implementation of the 2014 peace accord, which ended decades of conflict between the Philippine government and Moro Muslim separatists. In 2019, a parliament was created to govern the Bangsamoro, with Philippine presidents appointing its members. Slightly more than half the seats were reserved for members of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, or MILF, the region’s largest Moro Muslim armed movement. Following four postponements of the vote over the last seven years – first because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and later due to a range of legal and political complications – residents will finally have the chance to elect all their regional parliamentary representatives. The fact that the vote is now taking place is an accomplishment in and of itself. Election fever has gripped the region since the campaign officially began in late July. Vehicles roam the streets with loudspeakers blasting party jingles, huge posters of candidates decorate Bangsamoro roads, and catchy slogans and vlogs saturate citizens’ social media feeds. With voters set to choose from twelve parties, and with 631 candidates jockeying for 80 parliamentary seats, the competition to attract public support has been fierce. Electioneering has a darker side, too, with some campaigns spreading disinformation about rival candidates and parties. The vote is set to deliver a long-awaited verdict on how well MILF candidates have handled the transition from conducting guerrilla warfare to administering the autonomous region. Over the last seven years, the MILF-led interim administration has achieved a number of modest results, for instance strengthening social services and reducing child mortality. That said, and despite residents’ high expectations at the start of the peace process, the people of the Bangsamoro are still among the poorest in the country. The elections also come at a moment of high tension within the movement’s ranks. In March 2025, the national government replaced Chief Minister Murad Ebrahim, the MILF’s chairman, with the movement’s top military commander Abdulraof Macacua, generating a schism in the organisation. During an assembly in early September, the Central Committee stripped Macacua and 40 other MILF military commanders of their official functions. Mohagher Iqbal, head of the peace implementation panel and MILF vice chair, remains loyal to the displaced chief minister, Murad. Who is taking part in the polls? Twelve political parties are competing. While some have laid out clear platforms, the majority have had little of substance to offer in their campaigns. Such is often the case in the Philippines, where political campaigns tend to centre around personalities, rather than policy platforms, given the weaknesses of the party system. Even so, a milestone in the Bangsamoro’s political life came on 27 August, when representatives from all parties took part in a six-hour public debate in Cotabato City on priorities for the future government. Broadly speaking, the political spectrum can be divided into three blocs. The first is made up of the ex-rebels, who are represented by three parties broadly reflecting the split at the heights of the MILF: the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), which is a vehicle for Murad; the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, which is led by Macacua but includes several senior MILF cadres and influential local politicians; and the ABOT party, which is comprised of Iqbal partisans. In addition to the troika of parties affiliated with the MILF, two parties have emerged from the Moro National Liberation Front, the Bangsamoro’s first separatist movement (from which the MILF split in 1977). Campaign posters of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party in Cotabato City, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht The second category consists of parties led by the region’s political clans, or families that dominate local politics and aspire to extend their reach across the region. The most notable is the Bangsamoro Grand Coalition, an alliance of powerful clan leaders associated with the Alonto-Adiong, Hataman and Mangudadatu families, whose members felt politically excluded during the MILF-led interim administration. Once the primary opposition to the ex-rebels, this coalition now faces competition from the Bangsamoro Federalist Party mentioned above, as well as the Progressive Bangsamoro Party, whose base is in the provinces of Sulu and Tawi-Tawi. The latter is linked to the Loong and Matba families. A third category encompasses smaller parties. Some of these are led by civil society figures who promise institutional reform and champion minority rights. The Raayat Party, for example, includes experienced lawyers and legislators who are pressing for transparency in government and better access to public services. The Indigenous, Settler, Sama and Minorities Alliance Party, which focuses on safeguarding the rights and interests of the region’s Sama minority, is also among the smaller parties that would bring valuable expertise and perspectives to the parliament. These two parties are, however, unlikely to win more than a handful of seats . Half the parliamentary seats will be filled via proportional representation, with voters casting ballots for party lists. Citizens across the region’s 32 electoral districts will also vote for district representatives, who will fill another 40 per cent of the seats. The remaining 10 per cent (eight seats) are reserved for “sectors”, also elected by popular vote – except in the case of non-Moro Indigenous communities, whose representatives have already been elected via community assemblies . Non-Moro Indigenous communities and Christian settlers will each hold two seats, while women, traditional leaders, youth and religious scholars (known as ulama ) will have one seat each. Once the elected parliamentarians take office on 30 October, they will elect the chief minister through a majority vote. Unless a single party wins more than 41 seats – an unlikely prospect – party leaders will therefore need to forge a coalition in order to form a government. Some locals suspect that President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr.’s administration favours an outcome that would preserve Macacua as leader, with his MILF faction governing in a coalition with dominant local clans. This suspicion is not unfounded, given the national government’s unexpected move in 2025 to place Macacua at the helm of the Bangsamoro government. Campaign posters of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party and the Bangsamoro Party in Cotabato City, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Philippines. August 2026. CRISIS GROUP / Georgi Engelbrecht How has the campaign played out? The UBJP has campaigned hard. Its strategy consists of harnessing grassroots support while building alliances with politicians who oppose the Grand Coalition and the Federalist Party. Leaders and senior cadres emphasise the importance of honouring the 2014 peace agreement in full. In rallies across the region, UBJP candidates have called for “moral governance”, a concept that infuses the notion of good governance with Islamic principles. Other parties also invoke religious language, but the UBJP is the only one using it as a pillar of its campaign. The Federalist Party, meanwhile, has focused on a message of “inclusion” and anti-corruption, while the parties associated with the MNLF highlight their movement’s early contribution to the Moro struggle. The Grand Coalition, for its part, is leveraging its clan-based network, which is led by the governors of Lanao del Sur and Basilan. The campaign has revealed an inherent contradiction at the heart of Bangsamoro politics. That is, despite the establishment of a parliamentary system – which is distinct from the presidential system used by the Philippines at the national level – and the concomitant creation of new political parties, clans and personalities still matter more than parties or issues. Established political families can leverage patronage, largesse and the campaign experience they have acquired thanks to national and local polls to garner voters’ support. Familial ties still shape party lists, and some clans are fielding candidates from different parties in order to ensure that they are installed in the region’s power structure no matter the vote’s outcome. “The electoral game, the innovations of the system, have already been rigged”, a former party aide lamented. Are conditions in place for a peaceful election? Electoral violence constitutes the biggest threat to these polls. Flare-ups are a staple of Philippine politics, and election-related murders are regular occurrences. The presence of armed groups and widespread proliferation of firearms mean that political violence is even more widespread in the Bangsamoro. In the Philippines’ 2025 elections for governors, mayors and national senators, more than a third of the violent incidents recorded nationwide took place in the Bangsamoro. In one incident during the mayoral election in the town of Hadji Mohammad Ajul in Basilan, a clash between warring clans claimed four lives. The Philippine Commission on Elections has designated almost 40 per cent of the region’s towns as being at high risk of violence. Multiple incidents have already occurred since the beginning of the campaign – including an attempted ambush on interim Chief Minister Macacua. It is, however, unclear who was behind the attack. Indeed, many locals believe it may have been staged in order to engender sympathy for Macacua and boost his Federalist Party’s chances. Direct clashes of the military and police with ex-rebels are unlikely, but shootouts and disturbances involving competing political camps and candidates are possible, including on election day. Two main risks stand out. First, contests for district seats – which involve individual candidates facing off against one another – can more easily tip into violence given the personal nature of the competition. Secondly, friction could arise between supporters of the UBJP and the Federalist Party, both of them offshoots of the ex-rebel MILF, as well as between the UBJP and the Grand Coalition, particularly in areas where all the major political forces are campaigning. Those who seek to threaten or attack rivals can deploy tried-and-tested tactics ranging from bombings on the eve of the polls to scare voters to attacks on polling booths. Crisis Group knows of at least one powerbroker who has allegedly prepositioned dozens of rifles in a Maguindanaon village. Inflammatory online posts and trolling, often involving prominent MILF-linked personalities representing different factions, could also help spur real-world violence. A young cadre warned that this escalation is “just a matter of time”. Campaign rhetoric has on occasion turned worryingly bellicose. During a Federalist Party rally in August, Macacua said the party “was prepared for war to ensure that the Bangsamoro is on the right path”. Though he did not specify the target of this warning, some locals perceived it as a threat to his former comrades. On 3 August, top MILF military leader Abdullah Macapaar – alias Commander Bravo, who remains loyal to the Central Committee – warned that opponents of his party might manipulate the polls. The following month, after state authorities intercepted MILF members under his command and sent them back to their camp, he declared in a speech: “If we are picked on, we will not allow ourselves to be bullied”. In terms of potential flashpoints, the greatest security risks lie in the province of Maguindanao del Sur and the Special Geographic Area, a cluster of eight municipalities near the regional capital of Cotabato City. In these locations, candidates include prominent MILF personalities and commanders, as well as traditional elites. For example, the son of MILF chair Murad Ebrahim will face off against Butch Malang, a senior MILF commander widely considered loyal to Chief Minister Macacua. Meanwhile, parts of Lanao del Sur province, which has a long history of political violence, are also vulnerable to flare-ups. The island province of Basilan also warrants close monitoring, given both divisions within the governing Hataman clan and internal MILF rifts. Given how prevalent vote buying is in the Philippines, many locals fear that victory will depend on which political bloc has the most cash to dispense. Whether the elections will be free and fair is another question. Given how prevalent vote buying is in the Philippines, many locals fear that victory will depend on which political bloc has the most cash to dispense. Pre-election assessments highlight this risk, warning that it could undermine the election’s legitimacy. Community leaders Crisis Group spoke to also expressed this view. The practice of command votes, under which influential local leaders tell entire communities whom they should vote for, presents another challenge. While mayors and governors are not running in this election, they have an interest in the fortunes of certain candidates, especially if members of their clans are competing. International and domestic entities are working to promote a free and safe poll. Diplomatic representatives of the European Union, Australia, Switzerland, Singapore and Japan will be present in Cotabato City and a handful of nearby locations. Local and international NGOs such as the Independent Election Monitoring Center in Cotabato City, the Legal Network for Truthful Elections, the International Republican Institute, the National Democratic Institute and the Asia Network for Free Elections , are also deploying across the region. They all aim to publish reports of their findings. The national government, moreover, will be dispatching thousands of soldiers and police to the Bangsamoro, with an eye to deterring election-related violence. Some locals , however, view the deployment as overly heavy-handed. What happens after the vote? The major question hovering over these elections is how the MILF and its various factions will fare. The Bangsamoro electorate already had a chance to vote for UBJP-aligned candidates during the 2022 general and local elections , the 2023 village elections , and the 2025 mid-term and local elections. The party’s performance was not impressive; its few successes relied in no small part on local elite backing (either from mayors or village chairs). The MILF’s internal divisions have weakened the UBJP’s chances even further, since they will splinter the vote for the ex-rebels: this time, many local powerbrokers appear to be siding with the Federalist Party or the Grand Coalition. As a result, the most optimistic forecasts say the UBJP will secure only a quarter of parliamentary seats, at best, and about a tenth at worst. While the party could join with smaller parties to muster a majority, the prospect of it being able to rally enough legislators to make up for a poor performance seems unlikely. A more probable scenario is that the Federalist Party or the Grand Coalition achieves a parliamentary majority, possibly with the support of other parties. Both would then back the election of Macacua as chief minister, though the distribution of ministerial positions would hinge on the vote’s outcome. (Parties that garner more votes will presumably lay claim to a greater share of cabinet appointments.) Whether the UBJP will be able to prevent a clan-based coalition from forming a government with Macacua by driving a wedge between the leading political families, or by persuading elected parliamentarians to defect to its ranks when the vote for chief minister takes place, remains an open question. Not surprisingly, some MILF members still hope for reconciliation among the movement’s leaders, though the prospect of that happening seems slim at this juncture. A major loss for the UBJP would be a significant setback for the MILF’s Central Committee. With the MILF leaders ageing, it would fall to mid-level commanders and cadres to build the party into a credible opposition force in the regional parliament over the next five years. A more immediate concern should the UBJP fare poorly is the potential for conflict. Should the MILF rank and file loyal to Murad come to believe that Macacua conspired with Manila to strip the UBJP of its win, aggrieved fighters might turn their frustrations on their former comrades or the national government. The MILF itself could also withdraw from official peace process activities and refuse to disarm. It could even dispatch its troops back to the region’s hills and jungles to express its frustration without resorting to fighting. While successful elections are a crucial step in the peace process, much of the agreement remains unrealised. While successful elections are a crucial step in the peace process, much of the agreement remains unrealised. Rebel and militia demobilisation are stuck in bureaucratic limbo. Manila has pledged to convert former MILF camps into “safe and prosperous communities” by building infrastructure such as roads and starting community-managed economic projects. That effort also lags behind schedule. The same is true of the accord’s transitional justice and amnesty provisions. The government and the peace panel of MILF’s Central Committee, which is aligned with the UBJP and has been in charge of the peace process for the former rebels, have agreed to meet in the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur after the vote to discuss implementation of the remaining points of the peace agreement. That might be a sign that Manila is committed to honouring the accord no matter how the elections turn out. Still, there is a growing risk that President Marcos, Jr. will not make the peace process a priority as his term in office starts to wind down. Should the MILF Central Committee’s influence further erode as the splits between ex-rebels widen, Manila may also see little reason to continue treating the movement as an equal partner. For residents of the Bangsamoro, meanwhile, the new regional administration will need to leverage its electoral legitimacy to institute policies that make a material difference in their lives. They are still anxiously waiting for the changes the peace deal promised to start delivering over a decade ago. Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027 eschelhaas Mon, 09/14/2026 - 10:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Candidates for United Nations Secretary-General position participate in a debate at the UN General Assembly Hall in New York, on July 23, 2026. Leonardo MUNOZ / AFP Special Briefing 15 / Multilateral Diplomacy 14 September 2026 20+ minutes Ten Challenges for the UN in 2026-2027 As the 2026 General Assembly begins, the UN remains hobbled by cost cutting and big-power wrangling. The new Secretary-General to be chosen soon cannot cure all that ails the organisation, but much can be done to put its still considerable capacity to work. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Full Report (en) Related Tags Global What’s new? Leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly will find an organisation in need of revival. UN diplomacy aimed at halting wars and easing civilian suffering remains paralysed, while funding cuts have weakened UN capacity. States have one eye to the future as they prepare to appoint a new Secretary-General. Why does it matter? The UN remains the only universal forum for global cooperation on war and peace, even as the international order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope the next Secretary-General can help the organisation dispel its malaise and forge a new direction. What should be done? A new Secretary-General cannot resolve the world’s crises overnight, but this person should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capabilities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. I. Overview When world leaders last met at the UN General Assembly in September 2025, the organisation was in disarray, reeling from U.S. aid freezes and major-power disputes. A year on, the organisation remains trapped in an open-ended crisis, even after an additional round of cost cutting and other reforms. Under the Trump administration, the U.S. has morphed from a flawed champion of the international legal order into an overt scofflaw. While the U.S. has not repudiated the multilateral system anchored by the UN, it has done great damage to the organisation, insisting on shrinking multilateral peace operations, slow-rolling funding and tried to impose its ideological agenda. The Security Council continues to be a forum for hashing out big-power differences – with the U.S., Russia and China coming to agreement on second-tier files. But as regards the most salient peace and security challenges today – the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, as well as Ukraine and Sudan – the UN is notable mainly for being stuck. The next Secretary-General cannot cure all that ails the UN, but creative diplomacy could be useful in putting its still considerable capacity to work. If the overall mood at the UN is one of drifting toward perdition, it is partly because everyone is waiting for change at the top of the system. Secretary-General António Guterres will complete his term at the end of December. A small batch of candidates – eight, at the time of writing – have been publicly and privately lobbying throughout the year to replace him. Most have been cautious in their campaigning, to avoid offending the major powers that dominate the selection process. UN insiders are watching with mixed feelings. Some hope that the next Secretary-General can bring new energy to the organisation and, assuming Washington is amenable, restore a measure of political relevance and financial stability. Others worry that the U.S., China and Russia will connive to choose a weak candidate firmly under their control and that the Trump administration will force the next UN chief to make even more radical cuts throughout the institution. The selection process has at least focused minds on what the UN, multilateral cooperation and international law exist to achieve. Many member states have emphasised that they would like to see the incoming Secretary-General do more to promote conflict prevention and resolution, which Guterres has sometimes given short shrift while pursuing other goals, such as international cooperation on artificial intelligence. Guterres no doubt felt that he had little to gain by focusing on geopolitical crises given the lack of consensus among the big powers. But there is now a widespread sense that the UN cannot pretend to be a useful platform for discussions of far-reaching issues like AI if governments do not believe that it can deliver on its core, UN Charter-defined purpose of maintaining peace and security. The crises of the last twelve months have also offered reminders of the extent to which the UN still offers a necessary if imperfect scaffolding for international cooperation. The Trump administration has grudgingly turned to the Security Council to endorse its conflict management efforts in Haiti and Gaza. Faced with the fallout of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, such as closure of the Strait of Hormuz, governments around the world have stressed the importance of international legal principles including the prohibition of aggressive war, rules protecting civilians and civilian objects in conflict, and freedom of navigation. Though the UN has had a vanishingly small voice in diplomacy aimed at ending the Middle East war, both U.S. and Iranian officials have acknowledged that the Security Council should play some role – if only a ministerial one – in any peace deal. The UN ... remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors ... can handle. These are small consolations, but at a moment in which the U.S. and Russia are learning the limits of hard power in the Middle East and Ukraine, there is still space to reiterate the case for diplomacy, cooperation and respect for law. The next UN Secretary-General can make it. While it is foolish to expect a single administrator, however senior, to save the world, many small and midsize UN member states, as well as many major-power officials, are ready to heed a call to reinforce the lapsing international legal order. The UN also remains best positioned to deliver humanitarian aid, mount peace operations and manage protracted crises that few other actors – including the flailing U.S.-backed Board of Peace – can handle. It is possible that new leadership at the UN can give the organisation as a whole, and its peace and security pillar in particular, a new strategic direction. But amid deadly violence, regional rifts and institutional headaches, it is a near certainty that UN crisis management will continue to involve a great deal of firefighting and muddling through. This briefing, based on Crisis Group’s research at the UN and in the countries concerned, offers a guide to some of the most urgent issues. II. The Year in Review: Trends in UN Diplomacy The UN spent much of the past year adapting to a more assertive and transactional U.S. administration. Alongside long-running crises in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, the latest U.S.-Israeli war with Iran placed additional strain on Council diplomacy and the UN-backed international order. 1 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°14, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Power , 8 July 2026. Meanwhile, the UN’s multi-year liquidity crisis worsened, compounded by the U.S. aid cuts, disrupting operations at headquarters in New York and in the field. Steep reductions in voluntary contributions to UN humanitarian agencies forced the organisation to make difficult choices with its assistance, leaving many civilians affected by armed conflict with little support. Debates over the UN’s future simmered as member states began their search for the next Secretary-General. A year after Donald Trump’s return to the White House, the organisation was no longer in shock but adjusting to a new normal. A. Crisis Management and UN Diplomacy 1. The Security Council A year ago, Crisis Group observed that U.S. diplomacy at the Security Council under the newly installed Trump administration had lacked a clear direction. 2 Crisis Group Special Briefing N°13, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , 9 September 2025. The arrival of U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz in New York on the eve of the 2025 UN General Assembly marked the beginning of a more purposeful, and often determined, U.S. approach in the Council. Together with Panama, the U.S. secured Council authorisation for a new Gang Suppression Force for Haiti shortly after Waltz’s arrival, along with a UN logistics office to defray some of the Force’s costs (see Section III.4). 3 “ Haiti: Vote on a Draft Resolution Authorizing a ‘Gang Suppression Force’ and a UN Support Office* ”, Security Council Report, 30 September 2025; Daniel Forti, “ New Force to Battle Haiti’s Gangs Gets Security Council Blessing ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 1 October 2025; Crisis Group Latin America & Caribbean Report N°110, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , 15 December 2025. Less than two months later, the Trump administration – backed by its regional partners and Palestine – persuaded the Council to endorse its ceasefire plan for Gaza and establish the vaguely defined Board of Peace. 4 “Resolution 2803”, UNSC S/RES/2803, 17 November 2025; Daniel Forti, Richard Gowan and Max Rodenbeck, “ What to Look for as the Gaza Peace Plan Comes to the UN Security Council ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 November 2025. In both cases, the Council agreed to arrangements that concentrated decision-making authority in Washington and minimised the UN’s political and operational roles. With UN diplomacy on the war in Gaza lowered to a simmer (see Section III.3), the U.S.-Iran conflict became the Council’s defining crisis of the past year. Major-power tensions over Iran were already high at the UN prior to the outbreak of hostilities at the end of February. After the breakdown of nuclear diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran in 2025 and the twelve-day campaign launched by Israel (and joined by the U.S.) against Iran in June, France, Germany and the UK – three of the participants in the 2015 nuclear deal, or Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action – decided to reimpose “snapback” sanctions on Tehran that were otherwise set to expire that October. 5 Naysan Rafati and Daniel Forti, “ Iran Sanctions Snapback at the UN ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 25 August 2026. Beijing and Moscow rejected the legality of the reimposed UN sanctions, and in protest, they have obstructed business in all of the Council’s sanctions committees and thematic working groups since 2026 began. 6 China and Russia have blocked the appointment of the chairs and vice chairs of all subsidiary bodies, which require Council unanimity according to the body’s informal working methods. The chairs and vice chairs are responsible for leading each body’s meetings, briefing the Council on behalf of each body and managing its workflow. For more, see “ In Hindsight: A Second Year of Delays in the Allocation of Subsidiary Body Chairs ”, Security Council Report, 1 July 2026; Letter from the Security Council’s ten elected members , UNSC S/2026/636, 30 July 2026. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. Tensions in the Council gradually escalated after the U.S. and Israel once again attacked Iran on 28 February. China and Russia sharply criticised the two states during the Council’s first emergency meeting on the war. But even so they allowed passage of a Bahrain-led resolution condemning Iran’s retaliatory fire at its Gulf Arab neighbours days later, abstaining instead of vetoing it. Their posture suggested that preserving relations with the Gulf states was a higher priority than blocking a one-sided resolution that had no teeth. 7 Beijing and Moscow abstained from the vote. Russia also submitted a separate counter-resolution discussing the war’s root causes that got too few votes to be adopted. See “ Resolution 2817 ”, UNSC S/RES/2817, 11 March 2026. Their stances gradually hardened, however, as Washington pressed the Security Council to consider more coercive measures against Tehran. In early April, the Gulf states and the U.S. tabled a resolution for the Council to endorse a vaguely defined multinational naval coalition that would be tasked with reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Moscow and Beijing vetoed the text despite intense lobbying by Gulf capitals, arguing that the resolution would have given the U.S. open-ended authorisation to escalate its campaign. 8 The vote took place hours after U.S. President Donald Trump shared a social media message threatening to annihilate Iran. During its explanation of vote, Russia invoked the Security Council’s 2011 open-ended authorisation of NATO-led military action in Libya as a comparison to the proposed Gulf-U.S. initiative. Crisis Group interviews, UN diplomats, April-May 2026. See also remarks by the Russian Federation, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10130th meeting of the United Nations Security Council”, UNSC S/PV.10130, 7 April 2026. Weeks later, the U.S. and Gulf states drafted another resolution to demand that Iran open and demine the strait, while threatening sanctions for non-compliance. Despite finding over 138 co-sponsors, the U.S. and Bahrain did not submit the text for a vote, as they could not secure the support of Russia and China. Council diplomacy on the file has since stalled. Complex and sometimes volatile relations among the U.S., China, and Russia continue to shape the boundaries of Council diplomacy beyond the Gulf. After the reversal of U.S. Ukraine policy in early 2025, when the Trump administration stopped sending arms to Kyiv to resist Russia’s all-out invasion, Moscow may have expected Washington to press the Ukrainian government to make concessions in negotiations to end the fighting. Instead, U.S. statements in the Security Council have criticised Russia’s full-scale invasion and called on the Kremlin to agree to an immediate ceasefire. 9 Remarks by the United States, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10166th Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10166, 8 June 2026. More often than not, U.S. and Russian diplomats have sparred over UN responses to crises in the Middle East and Africa. By contrast, Washington and Beijing have shown willingness to strike occasional deals in the Security Council. Though they frequently clash, recent Council action has depended on a degree of cooperation between these geopolitical rivals. In September 2025, the U.S. agreed to pay nearly $680 million to the UN peacekeeping budget and drop its objections to China becoming penholder on the Council’s Afghanistan file in exchange for Beijing’s support for the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. 10 Daniel Forti and Richard Gowan, “ Reading the Signals of China’s U.N. Security Council Role in the Afghanistan Mission Renewal ”, Just Security , 31 July 2026. U.S. diplomats also convinced their Chinese counterparts to support the delisting of Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa and Interior Minister Anas Khattab from the UN counter-terrorism sanctions list despite Beijing’s reservations. 11 Maya Ungar, “ UN Lifts Sanctions on Syria’s President as White House Visit Beckons ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 7 November 2025. More recently, China and the U.S. collaborated to streamline the mandate of the UN political office in Afghanistan and approved each other’s candidates for leadership posts in UN missions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Sudan. Other Council members have found it harder to haggle with – much less criticise – the Trump administration’s adventurism. For the UK, France and many of the Council’s ten elected members, the importance of preserving bilateral relations with Washington has often quashed the temptation to toss rhetorical barbs at their U.S. counterparts. The repressed anger was most evident during the Council’s first meeting in January, an emergency session called shortly after the U.S. abducted former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, when many diplomats stopped short of censuring the Trump administration by name or condemning its action, though many took the view that the raid contravened international law. 12 “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10085th Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10084, 5 January 2026; Richard Gowan, “ Trump May Not Need a ‘Board of Peace.’ He Has the U.N. Under His Thumb ”, World Politics Review , 17 March 2026. Less than two months later, a majority of Council members only obliquely chastised the U.S. and Israel for their strikes on Iran, though many again saw the bombing as contravening the international legal order. 13 In addition to China and Russia, elected members Colombia and Pakistan also expressed strong reservations about the war. Richard Gowan, “ UN Security Council Members Limit Criticism of U.S. over Iran ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 2 March 2026. U.S. and French diplomats had a public spat at the end of July following the General Assembly’s re-election of Volker Türk as UN human rights commissioner, but the animosity has not lingered. 14 The U.S. was one of ten states to oppose Türk’s re-election in the 24 July UN General Assembly vote. In response, the Permanent Mission of France to the UN in Geneva criticised the Trump administration in a social media post by saying, “The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore”. Tweet by the French Permanent Mission to the UN in Geneva, @FranceONUGeneve, 1:12pm, 25 July 2026. In response, U.S. diplomats accused France of “disingenuous grandstanding” and walked out of the Security Council’s 27 July meeting on Ukraine as the French Permanent Representative to the UN delivered the country’s statement. See remarks by U.S. alternate representative to the UN, “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10202nd Meeting of the United Nations Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10202, 27 July 2026. London and Paris have tended to lobby Washington behind the scenes when they disagreed with the U.S. in Council debates. They avoided a showdown in the Council on the fourth anniversary of Russia’s all-out aggression against Ukraine in February, in contrast to a major row over a U.S. resolution calling for a rapid peace deal the year before, though U.S. and European diplomats still wrangled briefly over a General Assembly resolution in support of Ukraine. 15 Richard Gowan, “ UN Vote Shows Enduring but Uneven International Support for Ukraine ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 25 February 2026. The elected members’ divergent interests have also played a prominent role in shaping Council dynamics. The elected members’ divergent interests have also played a prominent role in shaping Council dynamics. Unusually, several elected members have found themselves directly implicated in issues before the Council in 2026 to date. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Somalia sought to preserve ties with the U.S. while influencing Council discussions on conflicts in their own countries. 16 Kinshasa has used its elected term on the Security Council to raise the profile of the conflict in the eastern DRC, while Mogadishu has sought to end the Council’s engagement with the war in Somalia. Denmark and Panama, meanwhile, have had to contend with Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and seize the Panama Canal, even as they maintained working relations with U.S. diplomats in New York. Bahrain assumed a more prominent role following Iran’s attacks on Gulf states, in close coordination with Washington. Colombia (under President Gustavo Petro, now out of office) and Pakistan, by contrast, have taken more critical positions on U.S. military actions. Whereas previous cohorts of elected members had found common ground in pressing Washington for a ceasefire in Gaza, the present elected ten are less unified in how to conduct diplomacy with Washington. As for UN peace operations, where Washington sees clear strategic interests at stake, such as in the DRC and South Sudan, it has been willing to preserve UN missions and, at times, moderate its normally reflexive opposition to human rights, gender and climate-related activities – including where it has been stubborn in other mandate negotiations in the Security Council and General Assembly. More often, the U.S. has sought to scale back UN operations, claiming concerns about their effectiveness and costs. Over the past year, it has pressed the Council to narrow the mandates of UN missions in Abyei (a disputed territory on the border between Sudan and South Sudan), the Central African Republic (see Section III.5), Colombia, Kosovo and Western Sahara, while supporting the closure of the UN mission in Yemen’s port city of Hodeida. 17 “ Yemen: Vote on Final Mandate Renewal of UNMHA ”, Security Council Report, 25 January 2026. It has also signalled its intention to terminate the mandate of the UN Support Office in Somalia, which provides logistical support to the African Union troops fighting Al-Shabaab, at the end of 2026. 18 Faisal Ali, David Lewis and Giulia Paravinci, “ Somalia peacekeeping mission at risk as US blocks UN support, sources say ”, Reuters, 2 July 2026. Despite U.S. scepticism, several Council members have mounted spirited defences of UN operations. During discussions to renew the mandate of the UN mission in South Sudan, European and African Council members succeeded in stopping the U.S. from deleting swathes of the UN peacekeeping operation’s mandate language on the political process and reducing the mission’s troop ceiling by several thousands. In late 2025, the Council’s three African members and Guyana (known as the A3 Plus coalition), together with China, Russia and Pakistan, were able to nix Washington’s proposal to predicate the renewal of the mandate for the UN peacekeeping force in Abyei on a series of harsh benchmarks. 19 “ UN Interim Security Force for Abyei: Vote on Mandate Renewal Resolution* ”, Security Council Report, 13 November 2025. Denmark and Pakistan (which work together in 2026 as an informal “peacekeeping duo”) negotiated intensely with U.S. counterparts to secure support for a thematic resolution to improve the UN’s accountability measures when its peacekeepers are harmed while serving in missions. 20 “ Resolution 2823 ”, UNSC S/RES/2823, 23 June 2026. South Korea, an elected member on the Council in 2024-2025, was the third member of this grouping, which previously was known as the “peacekeeping trio”. Crisis Group interviews, UN diplomats, May-June 2026. These examples suggest that when members show unity and coordination – and when they are not confronting what Washington sees as its core interests – they can sometimes engage in effective diplomacy with the U.S. 2. The Secretary-General Secretary-General Guterres has spent much of his final year in office trying to forestall the UN’s urgent financial crisis (discussed below), complete reforms under the UN80 initiative that he launched in 2025 and defend the UN Charter in response to violations by two permanent members, Russia and the U.S. 21 The UN80 initiative, launched by Guterres in March 2025, is premised on three separate reform processes. The first is premised on budget cuts and cost savings at the UN Secretariat; the second features a review of all inter-governmental mandates; and the third is anchored in proposals for larger institutional reforms (including proposals to merge different UN agencies and offices). “ UN80 Initiative ”, UN, August 2026. Neither Moscow nor Washington is eager to engage with him personally, curtailing his opportunities to pursue new diplomatic efforts. But the Secretary-General’s cautious outlook toward UN-led conflict management has left many diplomats and officials searching for a successor who will put the organisation’s work on peace and security front and centre. The Secretary-General’s limited influence over the past year has not always been due to a lack of initiative. Shortly after the resumption of hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, Guterres appealed for creating a humanitarian corridor to permit the passage of fuel and fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz, established a UN mechanism modelled on the Black Sea Grain Initiative to facilitate these efforts and appointed a personal envoy to boost the UN’s diplomatic response. 22 “ Note to Correspondents: on the Strait of Hormuz ”, UN, 27 March 2026. His focus on the war’s global consequences won plaudits but failed to have meaningful impact, as neither the Gulf states nor the U.S. showed serious interest in reopening the strait, except in full and without condition. The initiative has faded from memory even as the war has reignited and traffic through the waterway remains constrained. 23 Guterres shared a brief update about the UN mechanism at a 24 August press conference. See “ Secretary-General’s Press Encounter – On the United Nations’ Efforts to Uphold Navigational Rights and Freedoms ”, Office of the UN Secretary-General, 24 August 2026. Elsewhere, Guterres has deployed his dwindling political capital selectively. At the end of July, he travelled to Cyprus to revive his long-running mediation between Greek and Turkish Cypriots. He also made personal appeals to Sudan’s belligerents in support of a proposed humanitarian ceasefire in Darfur. The Secretary-General continued to press for Security Council reform, including at a high-level summit convened by France and Kenya in May, and in August he released a long-awaited review of UN peace operations mandated by the 2024 Pact for the Future (see Section III.9). 24 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations Peace Operations ”, UNGA A/80/798 – UNSC S/2026/600, 22 July 2026. Yet meaningful progress on these and other such priorities has eluded him. B. UN Reform The UN’s financial outlook has deteriorated sharply over the past year, largely due to Washington’s failure to pay its fair share. Since President Trump returned to office, the U.S. has ponied up only a portion of the nearly $4 billion in dues it owes the organisation. 25 In late August, the U.S. agreed to make a payment of $725 million to the UN regular budget, an amount reportedly calculated by Washington to avoid losing its vote in the General Assembly under Article 19 of the UN Charter. The U.S. is not the only member state withholding its obligatory dues, even if it is the largest and has accumulated the most arrears. China has regularly delayed its annual payments to the UN regular budget – in 2026 paying only at the beginning of September – though it traditionally does not accumulate arrears. C. The Search for a New Secretary-General The process of choosing Guterres’ successor, which began in November 2025, is approaching a crescendo. Members of the Security Council held their first straw poll at the end of July, and they will continue to take these informal soundings until one candidate receives at least nine votes from the fifteen-member body with no objection from any of the five permanent members. Eight candidates are in the running. They are: Ivonne A-Baki (former Ecuadorian ambassador to France and the U.S.), Michelle Bachelet (former president of Chile and head of UN Women), María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés (former foreign minister of Ecuador and president of the 73rd General Assembly), Rafael Grossi (director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency), Rebeca Grynspan (former second vice president of Costa Rica and head of the UN Conference on Trade and Development), Olara Otunnu (former Ugandan foreign minister and former UN representative for children and armed conflict), Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett (Guyana’s permanent representative to the UN) and Macky Sall (former president of Senegal). 39 María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés currently serves on Crisis Group’s Board of Trustees.
